concept.name: Sponsored access
concept.definition: A form of market access in which a customer or other person trades on an exchange or alternative trading system through the use of a broker-dealer's market participant identifier. SEC Rule 15c3-5 (the Market Access Rule) requires brokers providing such access to maintain, under their direct and exclusive control, risk management controls that prevent orders exceeding pre-set credit or capital thresholds and erroneous orders.
concept.intuition: The customer trades under the sponsoring broker's name and clearing umbrella, so the broker must police every order at the gateway.
concept.mechanics: Orders flow to the venue under the sponsor's MPID through automated pre-trade financial and regulatory filters; the sponsor must document and annually review the controls, with CEO certification, and may allocate only certain regulatory controls to broker-dealer customers by written contract after due diligence.
concept.failure_modes: Misconfigured filters, or impermissible delegation of control, can let erroneous or uncreditworthy orders reach the market at full speed; regulatory responsibility remains with the sponsoring broker-dealer regardless of allocation arrangements.
concept.misconceptions: Sponsored access is not unfiltered 'naked' access - since Rule 15c3-5, unfiltered access arrangements are prohibited in US securities markets.
concept.example: A proprietary trading firm routes orders to an exchange via its sponsor broker's MPID; the broker's gateway rejects any order that would breach the firm's pre-set capital threshold.

citations.source: 17 CFR 240.15c3-5 - Risk management controls for brokers or dealers with market access
